questions.question: Why does a single-node key-value store use a write-ahead log (WAL)?
options: To speed up read operations by caching recent writes
To ensure durability — data can be recovered by replaying the log after a crash
To compress data before writing to the hash map
To replicate data to backup nodes automatically
questions.explanation: A write-ahead log persists every write to disk before updating the in-memory hash map. If the node crashes, the in-memory state is lost, but the WAL can be replayed to reconstruct it. This guarantees durability without the overhead of flushing the entire hash map to disk on every write.

questions.question: In a distributed key-value store, what does consistent hashing provide?
options: Encryption of keys during transit between nodes
Partitioning of data across nodes with minimal redistribution when nodes change
Automatic compression of values to save storage
Guaranteed ordering of all write operations
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing maps keys to nodes on a hash ring. When a node joins or leaves, only the keys in the affected range need to move — roughly 1/N of the total data. This is far better than naive modulo hashing which reshuffles nearly all keys.

questions.question: What is the purpose of replicating data to multiple nodes in a distributed key-value store?
options: To reduce the size of each key-value pair
To provide fault tolerance — data survives even if some nodes fail
To increase the hash ring size for better distribution
To ensure all writes happen in a single round trip
questions.explanation: Replication ensures that if one node fails, copies of its data exist on other nodes. With N=3 replicas, the system can tolerate up to 2 node failures without data loss, providing high availability and durability.

questions.question: In a quorum system with N=3, W=2, R=2, what does the rule R+W>N guarantee?
options: All writes complete in under 2 milliseconds
At least one node in a read quorum has the latest written value
Exactly two copies of each key exist at all times
Reads and writes never happen on the same node simultaneously
questions.explanation: When R+W>N, the read set and write set must overlap by at least one node. This means any read quorum is guaranteed to include at least one node that participated in the most recent successful write, ensuring the latest value is always discoverable.

questions.question: How does the gossip protocol detect node failures in a distributed key-value store?
options: A central coordinator pings every node every second
Each node periodically exchanges heartbeats with random peers and tracks response failures
Nodes write health status to a shared database every minute
The load balancer removes nodes that return errors
questions.explanation: In gossip protocol, each node periodically picks a random peer and exchanges membership information including heartbeat counters. If a node's heartbeat hasn't incremented within a timeout, it's marked as suspected failed. This decentralized approach scales well and has no single point of failure.

questions.question: What is 'read repair' in a distributed key-value store?
options: Retrying a failed read operation on a different node
Detecting stale replicas during a read and pushing the latest value to them
Repairing corrupted data by comparing checksums
Redirecting reads to the primary replica when secondaries are overloaded
questions.explanation: During a read, the coordinator queries multiple replicas and compares responses. If some replicas return an older version, the coordinator sends the latest version to those stale replicas in the background. This opportunistic repair keeps replicas converging toward consistency without dedicated sync jobs.

questions.question: How do vector clocks detect concurrent conflicting writes?
options: By comparing wall-clock timestamps from each node
By tracking a logical counter per node — if neither vector dominates the other, the writes are concurrent
By hashing the write values and comparing the outputs
By locking the key globally before each write
questions.explanation: A vector clock is an array of counters, one per node. Each node increments its own counter on writes. If vector A has all counters >= vector B's, A happened after B. If neither dominates, the writes are concurrent and a conflict exists. This detects conflicts without relying on synchronized physical clocks.

questions.question: In a distributed KV store with N=3, what are the trade-offs of setting W=1, R=3 versus W=2, R=2?
options: W=1,R=3 has faster writes but slower reads; W=2,R=2 balances both
W=1,R=3 provides stronger consistency than W=2,R=2
W=1,R=3 uses less storage than W=2,R=2
There is no practical difference between the two configurations
questions.explanation: W=1 means writes succeed after just one replica acknowledges, making writes very fast but requiring all three replicas for reads (R=3) to guarantee seeing the latest value. W=2,R=2 balances latency more evenly. Both satisfy R+W>N for strong consistency, but availability characteristics differ.

questions.question: How do Merkle trees enable efficient anti-entropy synchronization between replicas?
options: They compress all key-value pairs into a single hash for quick comparison
They organize hashes in a tree so replicas can identify exactly which key ranges differ by comparing only O(log N) hashes
They encrypt data before synchronization to prevent eavesdropping
They automatically delete duplicate keys across replicas
questions.explanation: A Merkle tree hashes data ranges at leaf nodes and combines hashes up the tree. Two replicas compare root hashes first — if they match, everything is in sync. If not, they traverse down the tree, comparing child hashes to narrow down exactly which key ranges differ. This identifies inconsistencies in O(log N) comparisons instead of scanning all keys.

questions.question: A distributed KV store uses sloppy quorum with hinted handoff. During a network partition, Node C is unreachable. What happens to writes destined for Node C?
options: The writes are rejected until Node C recovers
Another node temporarily accepts writes on behalf of Node C and forwards them when C recovers
The writes are sent to all remaining nodes equally
The coordinator retries indefinitely until Node C responds
questions.explanation: With sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, when Node C is unreachable, a different node (say Node D) temporarily stores the writes with a 'hint' that they belong to Node C. When C recovers, D sends the hinted writes to C. This improves write availability during partitions at the cost of temporary inconsistency.
